content.title: Total, Average and Marginal Revenue

sections.title: Total Revenue
sections.keyIdea: Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity: everything the firm takes in from selling, before a single cost is taken off.

body.text: **Total revenue** is what a firm receives from selling its output. One formula, and it is the one the specification opens the topic with: **TR = P × Q**.
Nothing has been paid out yet. Revenue is not profit, is not what the owners keep and is not money in the bank — it is the top line, and every cost in the rest of this topic is taken off it.
Nadira Textiles sells cloth by the roll. At $32 a roll it sells 4 rolls a day, so total revenue is $32 × 4 = $128. Drop the price to $20 and it sells 10, so total revenue is $200.

That second figure is the interesting one. Cutting the price more than doubled what the firm takes in — and cutting it again, to $8, brings total revenue back down to $128. Total revenue rises, peaks and falls as the price comes down, and the rest of this chapter is about why.

realExample.text: A market trader who sells out by midday has high revenue and may have set the price too low; a trader with stock left at closing time may have set it too high. Neither knows from the day's takings alone, because takings are a product of two numbers that move in opposite directions.

sections.misconception: Students treat total revenue as what the firm "makes" and go on to talk about profit. Revenue is the whole amount received, before any cost at all. Instead write: total revenue is price times quantity, and profit is what is left after total cost has been taken off it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation, and advises showing workings. Quantitative skill QS6 at International Advanced Level is to calculate cost, revenue and profit, marginal, average and totals, so a revenue figure is something you will be asked to produce rather than only to discuss.

recall.prompt: Complete the three revenue formulae this chapter is built on:
template: Total revenue = P × ___
Average revenue = total revenue ÷ Q, which always equals the ___
Marginal revenue = the change in total revenue from selling ___ more unit
hints: what P is multiplied by
what average revenue always turns out to be
how many extra units a MARGINAL measure is about

sections.title: Average Revenue Is the Price
sections.keyIdea: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which is always the price — so the firm's demand curve and its average revenue curve are the same line.

body.text: **Average revenue** is total revenue divided by quantity: **AR = TR ÷ Q**. Put TR = P × Q into it and the Q cancels, leaving **AR = P**. Average revenue is the price, always, and not sometimes.

Start with the easier case. Suppose the firm can sell as much as it likes at one price — the price does not change however much it produces. Then every roll brings in the same amount, so the average brings in that amount and so does the next one: **AR = MR = P**, and all three are one horizontal line.

Now the case Nadira Textiles is in. To sell more rolls it has to lower the price, and not only on the extra roll — on all of them. Its demand line is **P = 40 − 2Q**, so average revenue falls as output rises, and the AR curve slopes downward.

The useful consequence: a firm's **demand curve is its average revenue curve** — one line with two names, because the price buyers will pay for a quantity is exactly the revenue per unit the firm gets.

realExample.text: A stallholder at a busy market is close to the first case: whatever they bring, they sell at the going rate. The only workshop of its kind in a town is in the second: to shift more work it must quote lower, to everybody.

sections.misconception: Students treat average revenue as something separate from price and look for a different figure. AR = TR ÷ Q = (P × Q) ÷ Q = P. Instead: read the demand curve as the average revenue curve, and stop looking for a second number.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define (2 marks) as requiring students to give the meaning of a term, concept or phrase. Two marks for average revenue means the formula and the fact that it equals price, not the formula twice in different words.

recall.prompt: Sort each statement by which case it describes:

groups.name: Price does not change with output
items: AR = MR = P at every quantity
The revenue curves are horizontal
Selling one more costs nothing on the units already sold
groups.why: With the price fixed, every unit and the next unit bring in the same amount, so the three measures coincide.

groups.name: Price must fall to sell more
items: MR lies below AR at every quantity above zero
The AR curve slopes downward
Selling one more means a lower price on every unit
groups.why: Lowering the price to sell one more applies to all the earlier units too, so what the extra unit adds is less than its price.

sections.title: Marginal Revenue Falls Twice as Fast
sections.keyIdea: Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from one more unit sold; on a straight-line demand curve it falls at twice the gradient and is zero where total revenue peaks.

body.text: **Marginal revenue** is the change in total revenue from selling **one more roll**: **MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ**. It answers "what did that last sale add?", which is not "what did it sell for?".
When the price must fall to sell more, the last sale adds its own price and takes a little from every roll already sold — so marginal revenue is below the price at every quantity above zero.
On a straight-line demand curve the arithmetic is exact: if **AR = a − bQ** then **MR = a − 2bQ**, the same starting point and twice the gradient. For Nadira Textiles, AR = 40 − 2Q and MR = 40 − 4Q.

steps.title: The firm lowers its price to sell one more
steps.subtitle: the lower price applies to every unit

steps.title: The extra unit adds its price
steps.subtitle: a gain

steps.title: Every earlier unit now sells for less
steps.subtitle: a loss, growing with output

steps.title: Marginal revenue is the gain minus the loss
steps.subtitle: below the price, falling twice as fast

body.result: At 10 rolls the two cancel: MR = $0, and TR is greatest at $200

body.text: Past that point MR is negative: one more roll takes total revenue **down**, the loss on the earlier rolls now exceeding the price of the extra one.

realExample.text: A workshop may find a bigger contract priced so low that it drags down what the firm can charge everyone else: worth something alone, and less than nothing once the other quotes are counted.

sections.misconception: Students write that marginal revenue falls "because the firm sells more". Selling more does not by itself lower revenue per unit: it falls because the extra sale requires a lower price on the units already sold. Instead: name that price cut.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a two-stage chain of reasoning: the price cut applying to all units, then the gain on the extra unit being smaller than the loss on the rest.

recall.prompt: Complete the relationship for a straight-line demand curve, and read it off Nadira Textiles's figures:
template: If AR = a − bQ then MR = a − ___bQ
Marginal revenue is $0 where total revenue is at its ___
Beyond that quantity marginal revenue is ___
hints: the factor that makes the gradient twice as steep
the top of the total revenue curve
what sign a number below zero has

takeaway: TR = P × Q. AR = TR ÷ Q, which is always the price. MR = the change in TR from one more unit.
A firm's demand curve IS its average revenue curve — one line with two names.
Where the price must fall to sell more, MR = a − 2bQ — twice AR's gradient, zero at peak TR.

content.title: Revenue and Price Elasticity of Demand

sections.title: Elastic, Unit Elastic, Inelastic
sections.keyIdea: Price elasticity of demand tells you what a price change does to total revenue, and it is the same fact as the sign of marginal revenue.

body.text: **Price elasticity of demand** measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price. It is negative, because the two move in opposite directions, and what matters is how far from zero it is.

items: **Below −1.00** — demand is elastic. Quantity responds more than price does, so cutting the price **raises** total revenue.
**Exactly −1.00** — unit elastic. The two changes cancel and total revenue does not move; this is where total revenue is at its greatest.
**Between −1.00 and zero** — demand is inelastic. Quantity barely responds, so cutting the price **lowers** total revenue.

body.text: Read "below −1.00" as further from zero: −3.00 is below −1.00, and −0.33 is above it. The minus sign is not a size.

Now put this beside the last chapter. Where demand is elastic, marginal revenue is **positive** and selling more adds to total revenue. Where it is inelastic, marginal revenue is **negative** and selling more subtracts. Where it is unit elastic, marginal revenue is $0.

These are not two topics that happen to agree. They are one fact about the next roll sold, written two ways — which is why the specification puts elasticity inside the revenue requirement rather than beside it.

realExample.text: A bus operator cutting fares on a route people can walk instead may fill the buses and take more money. The same cut on a route with no alternative fills nothing extra and simply collects less from the same passengers.

sections.misconception: Students say a price cut always increases revenue because more is sold. More is always sold; whether revenue rises depends on whether the extra quantity outweighs the lower price on every unit. Instead: state the elasticity first, then the revenue effect follows from it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a chain of reasoning, diagrams where appropriate, and depth rather than breadth. A chain that stops at "demand is elastic" has not reached the revenue, which is what the question asked about.

recall.prompt: Match each value of price elasticity of demand to what a PRICE CUT does:

pairs.why: Further from zero than one, so quantity responds more than price and the extra sales more than replace the lower price.
The two percentage changes are equal and opposite, so what is gained on quantity is exactly lost on price.
Closer to zero than one, so quantity hardly responds and the lower price is collected on almost the same number of units.

sections.title: Calculating PED, and the Revenue Effect
sections.keyIdea: PED is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, each measured against the value it started from.

body.text: The formula is **PED = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP**, and each percentage change is measured against the value it started from. Two worked cases, both on Nadira Textiles's single demand line, both a $2 price cut.
**The elastic end.** Price falls from $30 to $28, so quantity rises from 5 to 6 rolls. %ΔQ = +20%. %ΔP = −6.67%. PED = +20% ÷ −6.67% = **−3.00**. Total revenue moves from $150 to $168 — it **rises**.
**The inelastic end.** Price falls from $10 to $8, so quantity rises from 15 to 16 rolls. %ΔQ = +6.67%. %ΔP = −20.00%. PED = **−0.33**. Total revenue moves from $150 to $128 — it **falls**.
Both cuts are $2. Both start from a total revenue of $150. One ends $18 up and the other $22 down, and the only difference is where on the demand line the firm was standing when it cut.
That is why elasticity is not a property of a **good**. It is a property of a **point**: the same demand line is elastic at the top and inelastic at the bottom.

realExample.text: A shop running the same percentage discount across everything it sells will find the discount pays for itself on some shelves and not on others, without anything about the shop or the discount having changed.

sections.misconception: Students calculate the percentage changes against the new values, or against an average, and get a different answer from the mark scheme. Unless a question asks for the midpoint method, measure each change against the value it started from. Instead: write the two starting values down first and divide by those.
sections.examMatters: Quantitative skill QS8 is to make calculations of elasticity and interpret the result, so the number alone is not the answer: saying whether demand is elastic and what that does to revenue is the part that carries the question. Appendix 6 advises showing workings for a Calculate.

recall.prompt: Put the four stages of a PED calculation into the order you carry them out:
correctOrder: Write down the price and quantity before the change
Work out each percentage change against its own starting value
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage
Say whether demand is elastic or inelastic, and what that does to revenue
why: Both percentages are measured against these two figures, so nothing can be worked out until they are written down.
Each change is divided by the value it started from, and mixing the two starting values is the commonest error.
PED is the quantity response over the price response, in that order — the other way round gives the reciprocal.
A number on its own answers nothing: the question is about the revenue, and the number is the route to it.

takeaway: Elastic (below −1.00): a price cut RAISES total revenue and MR is positive.
Inelastic (between −1.00 and zero): a price cut LOWERS total revenue and MR is negative.
PED = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP, each measured against its starting value.
Elasticity is a property of a POINT on a demand curve, not of a good.

content.title: Diminishing Returns and the Product Curves

sections.title: The Law of Diminishing Returns
sections.keyIdea: In the short run at least one factor is fixed, so adding more of a variable factor eventually adds less and less extra output.

body.text: The **short run** is the period in which at least one factor of production cannot be changed. For Bahri Bottling that factor is the plant: it can hire another worker today and it cannot build another plant today.

The **law of diminishing returns** says that as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed one, the extra output from each additional unit of the variable factor eventually falls. The specification also calls this **diminishing marginal productivity**, and derives the whole short-run cost picture from it.

Watch it happen. The first worker at Bahri Bottling has the plant to themselves and produces 4 crates. The second adds 6 — more than the first, because two people can share the tasks. The third adds 5. The fourth adds 3. The fifth adds 2.

Nothing has changed about the workers. They are equally capable and equally willing. What has changed is how much plant each of them has to work with, and that is the whole of the mechanism: **the fixed factor is being spread thinner**.
Note the word **eventually**. Returns can rise first, and here they do — the second worker adds more than the first. Diminishing returns set in from the third onward.

realExample.text: A second cook in a small kitchen roughly doubles what comes out. A fourth is queueing for the same hob, and a fifth is standing in the way of the other four. The kitchen, not the cook, is what ran out.

sections.misconception: Students say output falls under diminishing returns. Total output usually keeps rising; it is the EXTRA output from each additional worker that falls. Instead: say marginal product falls, and be clear that total product can still be increasing while it does.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a two-stage chain of reasoning. Here the first stage is that a factor is fixed and the second is that each extra worker therefore has less of it to work with.

recall.prompt: Complete the law as the specification states it:
template: In the ___ run at least one factor of production is fixed
As more of a ___ factor is added to it
The extra output from each additional unit eventually ___
hints: the period in which the plant cannot be changed
the opposite of fixed
the direction that makes these returns "diminishing"

sections.title: Marginal Product and Average Product
sections.keyIdea: Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker; average product is output per worker; and marginal product crosses average product at average product's highest point.

body.text: Two measures, both about the variable factor. **Marginal product** is the extra output from one more worker: **MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL**. **Average product** is output per worker: **AP = TP ÷ L**.
At Bahri Bottling: marginal product rises to 6 crates at the second worker, then falls to 5, 3 and 2. Average product rises to 5 and holds it at the third worker, then falls to 4.5 and 4.
Look at the third worker. Marginal product is 5 and average product is 5 — they are **equal**, and that is exactly where average product stops rising.

steps.title: The next worker adds more than the current average
steps.subtitle: so the average is pulled up

steps.title: The next worker adds exactly the average
steps.subtitle: so the average does not move — its highest point

steps.title: The next worker adds less than the average
steps.subtitle: so the average is pulled down

body.result: Marginal product cuts average product from above, at average product's highest point

body.text: This is not a fact about Bahri Bottling's numbers. It is true of **any** average and its marginal: a value above the average raises it, a value below lowers it, and a value equal to it leaves it alone. The same argument returns twice more in the next chapter, for cost.

realExample.text: A batter's average rises when they score more than it and falls when they score less. Nobody has to calculate anything for that to be true — it follows from what an average is.

sections.misconception: Students learn "marginal cuts average at its minimum" and apply it to product curves, where average product has a maximum rather than a minimum. The rule is that marginal cuts average at its TURNING POINT. Instead: work out from the pulling-up and pulling-down argument which way the curve turns.
sections.examMatters: Quantitative skill QS4 is to construct and interpret a range of standard graphical forms and QS9 is to interpret information in tabular and numerical forms — and a product schedule is both.

recall.prompt: Put these four stages of the hiring process into the order in which they occur as workers are added to a fixed plant:
correctOrder: Every new worker adds more than the one before
One worker adds exactly what the workforce averages
Later hires each add less than the hire before
The final worker adds almost nothing to total output
why: Early on there is plenty of plant per worker and tasks can be shared, so extra output per worker is still growing.
At this point the extra output equals output per worker, which is where output per worker stops rising.
The fixed plant is now spread thinner with every hire, so each one has less to work with than the last.
Total output has nearly levelled off, and another hire adds cost without adding anything worth having.

sections.title: From Product to Cost
sections.keyIdea: Marginal cost is the wage divided by marginal product and average variable cost the wage divided by average product, so the cost curves are the product curves upside down.

body.text: The specification asks for the short-run cost curves to be **derived** from diminishing marginal productivity rather than drawn beside it. Here is how.

Each worker at Bahri Bottling costs $60 a day. The cost of the extra crates a worker brings is that wage spread over however many that is: **MC = wage ÷ MP**. Spread over output per worker instead: **AVC = wage ÷ AP**.

Check the second worker, where marginal product peaks at 6: MC = $60 ÷ 6 = $10, the **lowest** marginal cost in the table. Check the third, where average product peaks at 5: AVC = $60 ÷ 5 = $12, the **lowest** AVC.

items: **Marginal product and marginal cost** move opposite ways. MP highest ⇒ MC lowest; MP falling ⇒ MC rising.
**Average product and average cost** — the wage links AP to average VARIABLE cost, AVC = wage ÷ AP, so AVC turns where AP turns. Average TOTAL cost carries falling fixed cost too, so it turns later.
**Total product and total cost**: total cost is $120 plus $60 a worker, rising in equal steps while total product rises in unequal ones. Where output climbs fast, cost per crate is low.

body.text: So the U-shaped cost curves are not a separate thing to memorise: they are the product curves seen from the cost side.

realExample.text: A delivery round done in an hour and a half costs half as much per parcel as the same round taking three. Nothing about the fuel or the wage changed — only how much got done.

sections.misconception: Students explain rising marginal cost by saying inputs get dearer. Here the wage never changes: marginal cost rises because each worker adds fewer units to spread it over. Instead: attribute it to falling marginal product.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a chain of reasoning and depth rather than breadth. The specification's chain is diminishing marginal productivity, then rising marginal cost, then the curve shapes.

recall.prompt: Match each relationship the specification names to what it means:

pairs.why: The wage buys one worker and the worker brings the marginal product, so the cost of one more unit is the wage shared over those units.
The same wage shared over output per worker gives variable cost per unit, which is why AVC turns where AP turns.
Total cost climbs by the wage with every hire while total product climbs by whatever that hire adds, which is not the same each time.

takeaway: Short run: one factor fixed, so a variable factor eventually adds LESS extra output.
Marginal product cuts average product at average product's HIGHEST point.
MC = wage ÷ MP and AVC = wage ÷ AP: the cost curves are the product curves from the cost side.

content.title: The Seven Cost Measures

sections.title: Total, Fixed and Variable Cost
sections.keyIdea: Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost; fixed cost does not change with output and variable cost does.

body.text: Three totals, one formula: **TC = TFC + TVC**.

items: **Total fixed cost** does not change with output. Bahri Bottling pays $120 a day for its plant whether it makes 0 crates or 20.
**Total variable cost** changes with output. Here it is the wage bill: $60 a worker, so $180 for three workers.
**Total cost** is the two added: at 15 crates, $120 + $180 = $300.

body.text: The word **fixed** means fixed with respect to **output**, not fixed forever and not unavoidable. A rent can rise; it is still a fixed cost, because it does not rise when the firm makes one more crate.

And fixed costs exist only in the short run. In the long run every factor can change — the plant can be sold, not renewed or replaced by a bigger one — so in the long run **there are no fixed costs at all**. That distinction does more work in this topic than any other, and the last chapter turns on it.

realExample.text: A workshop's rent, insurance and the loan on its machinery arrive whether it runs one shift or three. Its materials and the wages of the shift arrive only if the shift runs. The first set is why closing for a week is not free.

sections.misconception: Students call any large or unavoidable cost fixed. The test is not size and not whether it can be escaped: it is whether the cost changes when output changes. Instead: ask what happens to this cost if the firm makes one more unit, and classify on the answer.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as requiring a calculation and advises showing workings. QS6 at International Advanced Level is to calculate cost, revenue and profit — marginal, average and totals — so all seven of this chapter's measures are examinable as arithmetic.

recall.prompt: Sort each cost Bahri Bottling pays into fixed or variable:

groups.name: Fixed cost
items: The rent on the plant
Insurance for the year
Interest on the loan that bought the machinery
groups.why: None of these changes when one more crate is made, which is the only test that matters.

groups.name: Variable cost
items: The wage of a worker hired for the day
Bottles and caps
Electricity used running the line
groups.why: Each of these arrives because a crate was made, and stops arriving if production stops.

sections.title: The Three Averages
sections.keyIdea: Average cost is total cost per unit, and it is average fixed cost plus average variable cost — a sum that holds at every level of output.

body.text: Divide each total by output and three more measures appear. **AC = TC ÷ Q**, **AFC = TFC ÷ Q**, **AVC = TVC ÷ Q** — and because TC = TFC + TVC, it follows that **AC = AFC + AVC** at every output without exception.

**Average fixed cost falls at every level of output, always.** The numerator never changes and the denominator only grows: $120 over 4 crates is $30 each, over 20 it is $6. It approaches zero and never arrives.
**Average variable cost falls, flattens and rises.** It is the wage divided by average product, so it turns where average product turns: lowest at $12, at 10 and 15 crates, then rising.

**Average cost is the two added together.** Early on the fall in AFC dominates and AC drops steeply, from $45 to $24. Later the rise in AVC takes over and AC turns up. So AC reaches its lowest point — $20, at 15 and 18 crates — **after** AVC reaches its own, and the gap between the two curves is average fixed cost, narrowing as output grows.
Check the arithmetic on any row: at 15 crates, $8 + $12 = $20.

realExample.text: A theatre's staging cost is the same whether forty people come or four hundred, so cost per seat collapses as the hall fills. Once it is full, extra performances need extra crew and cost per seat climbs again.

sections.misconception: Students draw average fixed cost as a curve that flattens out at some positive level, or turns up. It cannot turn up: a constant divided by a growing number falls forever. Instead: draw it falling towards the horizontal axis without ever touching it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Draw as requiring a diagram, and a cost diagram with AC and AVC drawn as parallel curves is not a diagram of these measures: the vertical gap between them is average fixed cost, so it must narrow as output rises.

recall.prompt: Complete the three average measures, then check them on Bahri Bottling at 15 crates:
template: Average cost = total cost ÷ ___
Average fixed cost always ___ as output rises
hints: what every average in this chapter is divided by
the direction a constant divided by a growing number moves
average fixed cost plus average variable cost

sections.title: Marginal Cost and Where It Cuts
sections.keyIdea: Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, and it passes through average variable cost and average cost at the lowest point of each.

body.text: **Marginal cost** is the addition to total cost from one more crate: **MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ**. Since fixed cost does not change, $120 of Bahri Bottling's total cost has no effect on it at all.
Down Bahri Bottling's table marginal cost runs $15, $10, $12, $20, $30. It falls while marginal product is rising and climbs once diminishing returns set in — the mirror image, through the wage.

Now the property every cost diagram turns on. Between 15 and 18 crates, marginal cost is $20 — and average cost is $20 at 15 crates and $20 at 18. Marginal cost has met average cost exactly where average cost is at its lowest, $20.

The reason is the pulling argument from the product curves, unchanged. While the next crate costs **less** than the current average, it pulls the average down. Once it costs **more**, it pulls the average up. So the average can only stop falling at the moment the two are equal.

It happens twice on one diagram: marginal cost cuts **average variable cost** at $12, its lowest point, and then cuts **average cost** at $20, its lowest point — and AC's minimum is further right, because average fixed cost is still falling and holding AC down after AVC has turned.

realExample.text: Adding a student to a class of twenty costs almost nothing and lowers cost per head. Adding one to a class of thirty-one means a second room and a second teacher, and cost per head jumps.

sections.misconception: Students draw marginal cost crossing average cost part-way up its rising section, or crossing AVC and AC at the same output. Neither is possible. Instead: put each crossing at the lowest point of the curve it crosses, AVC's to the LEFT of AC's.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Draw as requiring a diagram. On a short-run cost diagram the two crossings are the markable features, in that order from left to right.

recall.prompt: Complete the rule that governs every marginal and average pair in this topic:
template: While the next unit costs LESS than the average, the average ___
While the next unit costs MORE than the average, the average ___
So marginal cost cuts average cost at average cost's ___ point
hints: what a below-average value does to an average
what an above-average value does to an average
the turning point of a U-shaped curve

takeaway: TC = TFC + TVC, and dividing each by output gives AC = AFC + AVC at every level of output.
Average fixed cost falls forever and never reaches zero.
The gap between AC and AVC IS average fixed cost, so it narrows as output grows.
MC cuts AVC at $12 and AC at $20, each at its lowest point, AVC's first.

content.title: The Long Run, LRAC and Minimum Efficient Scale

sections.title: Short Run and Long Run
sections.keyIdea: The short run is the period in which at least one factor is fixed; the long run is the period in which all factors can be varied, so there are no fixed costs.

body.text: The two periods are not lengths of time. They are defined by **what can change**.

items: **Short run** — at least one factor is fixed. Bahri Bottling can hire and release workers; it cannot change the plant. Output is raised by working the existing plant harder, which is why diminishing returns bite.
**Long run** — every factor can be varied, including the plant. Output is raised by building the plant the output needs. Nothing is fixed, so **there are no fixed costs**.

body.text: How long that is depends on the industry, not the calendar. For a firm renting a small unit the long run may be a month; for one building a refinery, a decade.

The consequence for costs is the one the specification names at 2d. Every short-run average cost curve belongs to **one plant size**, and the long-run curve is the lower edge of all of them: for each output, the cost of making it in the plant best suited to it.
So the long-run curve can never lie **above** a short-run one: the firm can always keep the plant it has, so the short run is one of its options.

realExample.text: A bakery doubling output this month adds a night shift to the ovens it owns; one doubling output over three years installs more ovens. The second is cheaper per loaf, and the first is the only one available today.

sections.misconception: Students give the short run a fixed length — six months, a year — and apply it to every firm. The definition is about the fixed factor, so it differs by industry. Instead: say which factor is fixed and for how long.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a two-stage chain. "Long run" alone is not a stage: the marks are for saying that all factors can be varied and therefore that the plant itself is a choice.

recall.prompt: Sort each statement into the period it describes:

groups.name: Short run
items: At least one factor cannot be changed
Diminishing returns apply
Fixed costs are owed whatever the output
groups.why: The fixed factor is the definition, and everything else here follows from it: more of a variable factor on a fixed one, and a cost that does not move with output.

groups.name: Long run
items: Every factor including the plant can be varied
Economies of scale apply
There are no fixed costs
groups.why: With the plant itself a choice, cost per unit depends on the scale the firm builds for, and nothing is owed regardless of output.

sections.title: LRAC and Minimum Efficient Scale
sections.keyIdea: Long-run average cost falls where there are economies of scale and rises where there are diseconomies; minimum efficient scale is the lowest output at which it reaches its minimum.

body.text: The long-run average cost curve has three stretches, two of them named by what causes them.

items: **Falling** — economies of scale. Cost per crate drops as the firm builds bigger: at Bahri Bottling, from $21 at 10 crates a day to $13 at 50.
**At its minimum** — the curve reaches $13 and holds it from 50 to 70 crates.
**Rising** — diseconomies of scale. Beyond 70 crates cost per crate climbs again, to $16 at 90.

body.text: **Minimum efficient scale** is the **lowest** output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum: 50 crates a day here, not 70, although cost per crate is the same there. It is the smallest the firm can be and still have all its economies of scale.
That is why it matters: it says how big a firm must be to compete on cost. Where it is small relative to the market many firms reach it; where it is large, few can.
And note what is **not** happening here. Along the long-run curve nothing is fixed at all, so the rising stretch is not diminishing returns arriving.

realExample.text: Cement, steel and glass are made in very large plants because cost per tonne falls to a scale most firms cannot reach. A sandwich shop reaches its own minimum efficient scale with one kitchen, which is why there are so many.

sections.misconception: Students read minimum efficient scale as the output where the firm is at its most profitable, or as the whole flat stretch. It is neither: it is the lowest output at which average cost reaches its minimum. Instead: find the minimum cost, then read off the FIRST output that achieves it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define (2 marks) as giving the meaning of a term. For minimum efficient scale, both marks are in the wording: the lowest output, and at which long-run average cost is at its minimum.

recall.prompt: Put these four stages of a long-run average cost curve into the sequence a growing firm meets:
correctOrder: Unit cost falls steeply as the firm builds bigger
The lowest attainable cost per unit is reached
That level holds over a range of outputs
Costs per unit climb as the firm becomes harder to run
why: This is the economies-of-scale stretch, where each increase in scale spreads a cost over more units.
The first output at which the minimum is reached is what minimum efficient scale names.
Nothing further is gained from size here, and nothing is yet lost to it.
Diseconomies of scale: the firm has grown past the point where its own organisation keeps up.

takeaway: The two periods are defined by WHAT CAN CHANGE, not by a length of time.
In the long run every factor can be varied, so there are no fixed costs.
LRAC is the lower edge of every short-run curve, so it can never lie above one.
Minimum efficient scale is the LOWEST output reaching the LRAC minimum: 50, not 70.

content.title: Economies and Diseconomies of Scale

sections.title: Internal or External?
sections.keyIdea: An internal economy of scale comes from this firm growing; an external one comes from the industry around it growing.

body.text: An **economy of scale** is a fall in long-run average cost that comes from producing on a larger scale. The specification's first requirement here is the distinction between two kinds, and it turns on one question: **whose growth caused the saving?**

items: **Internal** — the saving comes from **this firm** growing. It arrives whether or not anything else in the industry changes, and it goes with the firm wherever it moves.
**External** — the saving comes from **the industry** growing, usually in one place. A firm that has not grown at all can gain one; a firm that leaves the area loses it however large it is.

body.text: The test is quick. Ask whether the firm would still have the saving if it stayed exactly the size it is. If yes, it is external. Ask whether it would still have it if every other firm in the industry disappeared. If yes, it is internal.

The distinction matters because the two are not equally reliable. An internal economy is the firm's own: it earned it and it keeps it. An external one belongs to a place and a moment, and can be lost to a road closing, a training college shutting or the other firms leaving — none of which the firm controls.

realExample.text: A textile firm that installs a bigger loom has lowered its own cost per metre. A textile firm in a town where a new technical college starts training weavers has also lowered its cost per metre, and did nothing to cause it.

sections.misconception: Students classify by size — big firm, internal; small firm, external. Size is not the test: a small firm in a strong industrial district enjoys external economies, and a large isolated firm enjoys none. Instead: ask whose growth produced the saving.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a two-stage chain. Naming an economy of scale is not a stage: the two are what the firm does differently at a larger scale, and why that lowers cost per unit.

recall.prompt: Sort each saving by whose growth caused it:

groups.name: Internal economy of scale
items: A bigger machine that only pays at high output
A lower rate of interest on a larger loan
A full-time specialist the firm can now justify
groups.why: Each of these arrives because THIS firm is larger, and the firm keeps it wherever it goes.

groups.name: External economy of scale
items: A college nearby now trains workers for this industry
A new rail head serves the industrial district
Firms in the district share research findings
groups.why: Each of these arrives because the industry around the firm has grown, and a firm that has not grown at all can gain it.

sections.title: Six Sources of Internal Economies
sections.keyIdea: The specification names six: financial, technical, managerial, marketing, purchasing and risk bearing.

body.text: Six, and the list is closed. Each is a cost that does not grow in step with output — it is paid once, borrowed once or hired once, and then spread.

items: **Financial** — a larger firm borrows at a lower rate of interest, because a lender treats it as a smaller risk.
**Technical** — a machine or a production run that only pays at high output spreads its cost over more units.
**Managerial** — a specialist manager is worth employing once there is enough output for the post to be full-time.
**Marketing** — one campaign, one design and one set of packaging artwork are paid for once and used across more units.
**Purchasing** — a supplier quotes a lower price a unit for a larger and more regular order.
**Risk bearing** — a firm selling several products in several markets is not ruined by one of them going wrong.

body.text: Learn them as six, with the mechanism attached to each. A question asking for two wants two named sources and what each does to cost per unit; naming four without explaining any is worth less.

Notice what they share. In every case the cost is **lumpy** — a loan, a machine, a manager, a campaign, an order, a product range — and a cost that rises exactly in step with output produces no economy of scale at all.

realExample.text: A drinks firm opening a second line buys its bottles on one larger contract, runs one campaign across both lines and borrows against a bigger balance sheet. Three of the six, from one decision.

sections.misconception: Students list sources without a mechanism — "technical economies of scale, so costs fall". The name is not the explanation. Instead: say what the firm does differently at a larger scale and why that lowers cost PER UNIT rather than in total.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain (4 marks) as requiring knowledge, understanding and application with a two-stage chain. Four marks is two sources, each taken as far as its effect on cost per unit.

recall.prompt: Match five of the six internal economies of scale to what produces each:

pairs.why: A machine or a production run that only pays at high output spreads its cost over more units.
A specialist manager is worth employing once there is enough output for the post to be full-time.
One campaign, one design and one set of packaging artwork are paid for once and used across more units.

pairs.right: a lower price a unit, larger order
pairs.why: A supplier quotes a lower price a unit for a larger and more regular order.
A firm selling several products in several markets is not ruined by one of them going wrong.

sections.title: Three Sources of External Economies
sections.keyIdea: The specification names three: the availability of skilled labour, access to transport links, and shared knowledge.

body.text: Three, and each belongs to a **place** rather than to a firm. They appear where an industry concentrates.

items: **Availability of skilled labour** — workers already trained for this industry live nearby, so hiring and training cost less.
**Access to transport links** — a port, a rail head or a trunk road near the industry lowers what it costs to move goods.
**Sharing knowledge** — firms in one place learn from each other, from their suppliers and from a shared research base.

body.text: They arrive together, which is why industries cluster and then keep clustering: the firms attract the workers, the workers attract more firms, and the transport and the training follow the demand. A firm arriving late gains all three on its first day.

And they can be lost without the firm doing anything. If the industry contracts, the trained workers move away, the freight service is cut and the shared research base closes — so a firm's cost per unit can rise while its own output, its own plant and its own management are exactly as they were.

realExample.text: Where an industry has concentrated for decades, a new entrant finds experienced workers already in the area, suppliers already delivering daily and a technical college already teaching the right skills. None of that is anything the entrant built.

sections.misconception: Students treat external economies as a firm being lucky, with no mechanism. Each one is a real cost that falls: less spent on training, less on freight, less on research. Instead: name the cost line the external economy reduces.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a chain of reasoning and depth rather than breadth. A chain about external economies has to reach the firm's own average cost, since that is what an economy of scale is defined as lowering.

recall.prompt: Complete the three sources of external economies of scale the specification names:
template: Availability of ___ labour
Access to ___ links
___ knowledge
hints: the kind of worker an established industry leaves behind it
what a port, a rail head or a trunk road provide
what firms in one place do with what they learn

sections.title: Three Sources of Diseconomies
sections.keyIdea: The specification names three sources of diseconomies of scale: communication problems, coordination problems and X-inefficiency.

body.text: A **diseconomy of scale** is a rise in long-run average cost that comes from producing on a larger scale. The specification names three sources, and all three are about the firm becoming harder to run rather than about anything it buys getting dearer.

items: **Communication problems** — a message crosses more people on its way, arrives later and arrives changed.
**Coordination problems** — more parts have to be kept in step, and the effort of keeping them in step grows faster than output.
**X-inefficiency** — costs drift above the lowest attainable level because nothing inside a large firm forces them down.

body.text: **X-inefficiency** is worth pausing on: costs drifting above the lowest level the firm could attain, not because anybody decided to waste anything but because in a large organisation nothing in particular forces them down.

Now the distinction students most often lose. **Diminishing returns** are a **short-run** effect: one factor is fixed and the variable factor is spread thinner. **Diseconomies of scale** are a **long-run** effect: nothing is fixed, the firm has built bigger, and the organisation itself is the problem.
They look alike on a diagram and share nothing underneath. If a question names a fixed factor it is the short run; if the firm has grown, it is the long run.

realExample.text: In a firm of ten, a problem reaches the person who can fix it the same morning. In a firm of ten thousand it crosses four departments first, arrives changed, and by then two of them have solved it separately and differently.

sections.misconception: Students explain diseconomies by saying workers become less productive as the firm grows, which is the diminishing-returns argument in the wrong period. Instead: name communication, coordination or costs drifting above the attainable minimum.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss as requiring a critical assessment with different viewpoints. Whether a firm should keep growing needs both sides of this curve, and which effect dominates over what range of output.

recall.prompt: Sort each description into the effect it belongs to:

groups.name: Diminishing returns
items: A short-run effect
At least one factor is fixed
More workers share the same plant
groups.why: The fixed factor is the cause, so this can only happen in the period where something cannot be changed.

groups.name: Diseconomies of scale
items: A long-run effect
Every factor including the plant has grown
Messages cross more people and arrive changed
groups.why: Nothing is fixed here: the firm has built bigger and its own organisation is what pushes cost per unit up.

takeaway: Internal economies come from THIS firm growing; external ones from the INDUSTRY around it.
Six internal: financial, technical, managerial, marketing, purchasing, risk bearing.
Three external: skilled labour, transport links, shared knowledge.
Three diseconomies: communication, coordination, X-inefficiency — all LONG run.

content.title: Profits, Losses and the Shutdown Points

sections.title: Normal Profit, Supernormal Profit and Losses
sections.keyIdea: Normal profit is where total revenue exactly covers total cost; above that is supernormal profit and below it is a loss.

body.text: Three outcomes, one comparison: **total revenue against total cost**, or equivalently **average revenue against average cost**.

items: **Normal profit** — TR = TC, so AR = AC. The firm covers everything, including what its owners could have earned elsewhere — the **opportunity cost** of staying in this business. That last part is why it counts as a profit at all.
**Supernormal profit** — TR > TC, so AR > AC: a return over and above what was needed to keep the firm in this line of business.
**Losses** — TR < TC, so AR < AC. Not enough to cover everything.

body.text: Bahri Bottling makes 15 crates a day at a total cost of $300, so average cost is $20. Read three prices against it:

items: At $26 a crate: revenue $390, cost $300, **supernormal profit of $90**.
At $20: revenue $300 against cost $300 — exactly equal, so **normal profit**.
At $16: revenue $240 against cost $300, a **loss of $60**.

body.text: Notice that normal profit shows as **zero** on the middle line. It is not zero reward — the reward is already inside the cost figure, and that is the hardest idea in this chapter.

realExample.text: Someone who leaves a salaried job to run a workshop has to earn that salary back before the workshop is worth running. One earning exactly that is doing fine, and earning no supernormal profit.

sections.misconception: Students read normal profit as the firm making no profit and conclude it will close. It covers every cost including what the owners could earn elsewhere, so there is no better use of their money. Instead: say it is the minimum return needed to keep the firm in this line of business.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define (2 marks) as giving the meaning of a term. For normal profit the two marks are the equality and what that cost includes — the opportunity cost of the owners' money and effort, which is the part most answers leave out.

recall.prompt: Match each comparison to what the firm is earning:

pairs.why: Every unit brings in more than it costs, so there is a return over and above what was needed to keep the firm here.
Revenue covers cost exactly, and that cost already includes what the owners could have earned elsewhere.
Revenue does not cover cost, and the next chapter decides whether the firm should still be producing.

sections.title: The Short-Run Shutdown Point
sections.keyIdea: In the short run a firm keeps producing while price covers average variable cost, because the fixed cost is owed whether it produces or not.

body.text: A loss-making firm has a decision, and it is not the obvious one. In the short run the fixed cost is owed **either way**: Bahri Bottling pays $120 a day for its plant even with the line switched off.
So the comparison is not "am I making a loss?" but **"which loss is smaller?"**. Shutting down costs the fixed cost, $120. Producing costs whatever the loss turns out to be.

**At $16 a crate.** Revenue $240, total cost $300, a loss of $60. That is worse than nothing and **better than $120**. Each crate covers its own variable cost of $12 and leaves $4 towards the fixed cost — $60 in all. So the firm keeps producing.

**At $10 a crate.** Revenue $150, a loss of $150 — **worse than the $120** of shutting down. Each crate now fails to cover even its own variable cost, so every one made adds to the loss. The firm shuts down.
**The short-run shutdown point is where price equals average variable cost**, $12 here. Above it, producing contributes something towards the fixed cost. Below it, producing makes matters worse.

realExample.text: A seaside hotel that opens through a quiet winter at rates well below its yearly running cost is not being foolish. The building is paid for either way, and winter guests cover the heating and the staff with something over.

sections.misconception: Students say a firm making a loss should shut down immediately. In the short run that costs the whole fixed cost, which is often the larger loss. Instead: compare the loss from producing with the fixed cost, and shut down only when price is below average variable cost.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a chain of reasoning and depth rather than breadth. The chain is the fixed cost being owed either way, then the contribution each unit makes, then the comparison of two losses.

recall.prompt: Put the four steps of the short-run shutdown decision into the order in which a firm works through them:
correctOrder: Note that the fixed cost is owed whether or not anything is produced
Ask whether the price covers variable cost per unit
Work out what each unit leaves towards the fixed cost
Compare the loss from producing with the loss from stopping
why: This is what makes stopping expensive rather than free, and it is the step most answers skip.
Variable cost per unit is the only cost that responds to the decision, so it is the only one the price has to beat.
Whatever is left over after variable cost is what producing contributes, and it is the reason to keep going.
The decision is between two losses rather than between a loss and nothing, and the smaller one wins.

sections.title: The Long-Run Shutdown Point
sections.keyIdea: In the long run there are no fixed costs, so a firm leaves the industry when price is below average cost.

body.text: In the long run **every** factor can be varied, so the plant is no longer owed: the lease ends, the machinery can be sold, nothing is renewed. There are **no fixed costs**.
That removes the reason for producing at a loss: with nothing owed regardless, there is no fixed cost to contribute towards. The comparison becomes revenue against **total** cost.
**The long-run shutdown point is where price equals average cost** — $20 for Bahri Bottling. Below that the firm leaves the industry.

steps.title: Price above average cost
steps.subtitle: supernormal profit: the firm stays and would expand

steps.title: Price equal to average cost
steps.subtitle: normal profit: covering everything, including what the owners could earn elsewhere

steps.title: Price between average variable cost and average cost
steps.subtitle: short run, keep producing; long run, leave

steps.title: Price below average variable cost
steps.subtitle: shut down at once, in either period

body.result: Two rules, two periods: short run, produce while price covers $12; long run, stay while price covers $20

body.text: Row three is the same firm at the same price being told two different things, and both are right: the rules answer whether to run the plant this month, and whether to be in this industry at all.

realExample.text: A workshop covering its wages and materials but not the lease will keep working to the end of the lease and then not renew it. Nothing changed about the workshop on the day it closed except which costs were still owed.

sections.misconception: Students apply the average variable cost rule to the long run and conclude a firm covering its variable costs never leaves. In the long run there are no fixed costs, so the test is average cost. Instead: name the period first, then choose the rule that belongs to it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring a judgement and different viewpoints. Whether a loss-making firm should close usually turns on how long the fixed commitment has left to run — a matter of period rather than arithmetic.

recall.prompt: Complete the two shutdown rules and the reason they differ:
template: In the SHORT run, shut down if price is below average ___ cost
In the LONG run, leave if price is below average ___ cost
They differ because in the long run there are no ___ costs
hints: the only cost that responds to the decision in the short run
everything the firm pays, per unit
what disappears once every factor can be varied

takeaway: Normal profit: AR = AC, the cost already including what the owners could earn elsewhere.
Short run: shut down below average variable cost ($12). The fixed $120 is owed either way.
Long run: leave below average cost ($20) — there are no fixed costs left to cover.

notes.title: Total, Average and Marginal Revenue
notes.keyIdea: The three revenue measures and the relationship between them.

items.text: Total revenue — TR = P × Q. Everything received from selling, before any cost.
Average revenue — AR = TR ÷ Q, which always equals the price. The demand curve IS the AR curve.
Marginal revenue — MR = ΔTR ÷ ΔQ: the change in total revenue from selling one more unit.
Where the price does not change with output: AR = MR = P, all three a horizontal line.
Where the price must fall to sell more: MR lies below AR, because the lower price applies to every unit already being sold.
On a straight-line demand curve AR = a − bQ and MR = a − 2bQ — twice the gradient. For Nadira Textiles, AR = 40 − 2Q and MR = 40 − 4Q.
MR = $0 at 10 rolls, where TR is greatest at $200. Beyond it MR is negative and selling more takes TR down.

takeaway: AR is the price. The demand curve and the AR curve are one line.
MR falls twice as fast as AR and is zero where TR peaks.
Revenue is the top line: no cost has been taken off it.

notes.title: Revenue and Price Elasticity of Demand
notes.keyIdea: Price elasticity of demand and its relationship to the revenue measures, including calculations.

items.text: Price elasticity of demand — PED = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP, each percentage measured against the value it started from. Always negative.
Elastic — below −1.00. Unit elastic — −1.00. Inelastic — between −1.00 and zero.
Elastic: a price cut RAISES total revenue, and marginal revenue is positive.
Unit elastic: total revenue does not move, and marginal revenue is zero. This is where TR is at its greatest.
Inelastic: a price cut LOWERS total revenue, and marginal revenue is negative.
Worked, on one demand line: $30 → $28 gives PED −3.00 and TR $150 → $168. $10 → $8 gives PED −0.33 and TR $150 → $128.
Elasticity is a property of a POINT, not of a good: the same line is elastic at the top and inelastic at the bottom.

takeaway: PED and the sign of MR are the same fact about the next unit sold.
Measure each percentage change against the value it started from.
The number is not the answer; the revenue effect is.

notes.title: Diminishing Returns and the Product Curves
notes.keyIdea: Diminishing marginal productivity, and how the short-run cost curves are derived from it.

items.text: Law of diminishing returns — as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the extra output from each additional unit eventually falls. Also called diminishing marginal productivity.
Marginal product — MP = ΔTP ÷ ΔL. Average product — AP = TP ÷ L.
Bahri Bottling: total product 0, 4, 10, 15, 18, 20 crates for 5 workers. Marginal product rises to 6 then falls; average product peaks at 5.
Marginal product cuts average product at average product's HIGHEST point: a value above an average pulls it up, a value below pulls it down, a value equal leaves it alone.
MC = wage ÷ MP and AVC = wage ÷ AP, so MC is lowest where MP is highest ($10) and AVC is lowest where AP is highest ($12).
TC = $120 + $60 × workers: total cost climbs in equal steps while total product climbs in unequal ones.
The U-shaped cost curves are not separate: they are the product curves seen from the cost side.

takeaway: It is the EXTRA output that falls, not total output.
The fixed factor being spread thinner is the whole mechanism.
Rising marginal cost comes from falling marginal product, not from a rising wage.

notes.title: The Seven Cost Measures
notes.keyIdea: The seven cost measures and how each relates to the others.

items.text: TC = TFC + TVC. Fixed cost does not change with output; variable cost does.
AC = TC ÷ Q, AFC = TFC ÷ Q, AVC = TVC ÷ Q, and therefore AC = AFC + AVC.
MC = ΔTC ÷ ΔQ — the cost of one more unit. Fixed cost does not affect it at all.
Bahri Bottling at 15 crates: TFC $120, TVC $180, TC $300; AFC $8, AVC $12, AC $20. $8 + $12 = $20.
Average fixed cost falls at every output and never reaches zero: $30 at 4 crates, $6 at 20.
MC cuts AVC at its lowest point $12 and AC at its lowest point $20 — AC's minimum lying further right because AFC is still falling and holding AC down.
The vertical gap between AC and AVC is average fixed cost, so the two curves converge and are never parallel.

takeaway: Fixed means fixed with respect to OUTPUT, not unavoidable and not large.
AC = AFC + AVC holds at every single level of output.
Marginal cuts average at the turning point, because of what an average is.

notes.title: The Long Run, LRAC and Minimum Efficient Scale
notes.keyIdea: The relationship between short-run and long-run costs, the LRAC curve, and minimum efficient scale.

items.text: Short run — at least one factor is fixed. Long run — every factor can be varied, so there are no fixed costs.
Minimum efficient scale — the LOWEST output at which long-run average cost is at its minimum.
Each short-run average cost curve belongs to one plant size; LRAC is the lower edge of all of them, so LRAC can never lie above a short-run curve.
Bahri Bottling's LRAC falls from $21 at 10 crates to $13 at 50, holds $13 to 70, then rises to $16 at 90.
Falling = economies of scale; rising = diseconomies of scale (3a). Minimum efficient scale is 50 crates a day — the FIRST output achieving the minimum, not the last.
Minimum efficient scale relative to the size of the market decides how many firms can compete on cost.

takeaway: The two periods are about what can change, not about how long.
LRAC is an envelope: the firm can always keep the plant it has.
Minimum efficient scale is the LOWEST such output.

notes.title: Economies and Diseconomies of Scale
notes.keyIdea: Internal and external economies of scale, their sources, and the sources of diseconomies.

items.text: Internal economy of scale — a fall in long-run average cost caused by THIS firm growing.
External economy of scale — a fall in long-run average cost caused by the INDUSTRY around the firm growing.
Diseconomy of scale — a rise in long-run average cost caused by producing on a larger scale.
Six internal sources: financial, technical, managerial, marketing, purchasing, risk bearing.
Three external sources: availability of skilled labour; access to transport links; sharing knowledge.
Three sources of diseconomies: communication problems, coordination problems, X-inefficiency.
Every internal economy is a LUMPY cost — a loan, a machine, a manager, a campaign, an order, a product range — paid once and then spread. A cost that rises in step with output produces none.

Diseconomies of scale are LONG run and come from the firm being hard to run. Diminishing returns are SHORT run and come from a factor being fixed. They look the same on a diagram and share nothing underneath.

takeaway: Ask whose growth caused the saving: the firm's, or the industry's.
Name the source AND the mechanism; the name alone is not an explanation.
X-inefficiency is the third source of diseconomies, and it belongs to 3.3.2.

notes.title: Profits, Losses and the Shutdown Points
notes.keyIdea: Normal profit, supernormal profit and losses, and the two shutdown points.

items.text: Normal profit — TR = TC, so AR = AC. The minimum return needed to keep the firm in this line of business; it shows as zero profit because the return is already inside the cost.
Supernormal profit — TR > TC, so AR > AC: anything above normal profit.
Losses — TR < TC, so AR < AC.
Bahri Bottling at 15 crates, TC $300: at $26 a crate, $90 supernormal profit; at $20, normal profit; at $16, a loss of $60; at $10, a loss of $150.
SHORT-RUN shutdown point: price below average variable cost ($12). The fixed $120 is owed either way, so the choice is between two losses — producing at $16 loses $60 against $120 for stopping.
LONG-RUN shutdown point: price below average cost ($20). In the long run there are no fixed costs, so there is nothing to contribute towards.
Between $12 and $20 the two rules disagree, and both are right: keep producing this month, leave the industry eventually.

takeaway: Normal profit is not zero reward — the reward is inside the cost.
Short run: compare price with AVC. Long run: compare price with AC.
Shutting down is not free in the short run; it costs the fixed cost.

quiz.question: Average revenue is always equal to:
options: marginal revenue, at every level of output
total revenue, at the quantity where it is greatest
the price
total cost divided by quantity
quiz.explanation: AR = TR ÷ Q and TR = P × Q, so the quantity cancels and average revenue is the price at every output. It equals marginal revenue only where the price does not change with output, and it has nothing to do with cost.

quiz.question: The law of diminishing returns applies:
options: in the short run, because at least one factor is fixed
in the long run, because the firm has grown too large to manage
in both periods, whenever output rises
only when the wage a firm pays is rising
quiz.explanation: Diminishing returns need a fixed factor for the variable factor to be spread over, and a fixed factor is what defines the short run. In the long run every factor can be varied, so rising cost per unit there is diseconomies of scale instead.

quiz.question: A firm earns normal profit when:
options: it makes no money at all from its activity
total revenue is exactly equal to total cost
its total revenue is greater than its total variable cost
it earns the same profit as other firms in its industry
quiz.explanation: Normal profit is TR = TC, and the cost figure already includes what the owners could have earned elsewhere. It shows as zero profit and is not zero reward, which is why a firm earning it has no reason to leave.

quiz.question: A firm faces the demand curve AR = 40 − 2Q. Its marginal revenue curve is:
quiz.explanation: If AR = a − bQ then MR = a − 2bQ. Same starting point, twice the gradient — because selling one more unit requires a lower price on every unit already being sold.

quiz.question: Total revenue is at its greatest at the output where:
options: average revenue is zero
marginal revenue is zero
marginal revenue is at its greatest
average revenue equals marginal revenue
quiz.explanation: While marginal revenue is positive, one more unit adds to total revenue; once it is negative, one more unit subtracts. The turning point is where it is exactly $0, which for this firm is 10 rolls and $200.

quiz.question: A firm that can sell any quantity it likes at the same price has revenue curves such that:
options: MR lies below AR at every output above zero
AR = MR = P at every output
AR slopes downward and MR slopes upward
MR is zero at every output
quiz.explanation: With the price unchanged by output, each extra unit brings in exactly the price and takes nothing away from the units already sold, so the average and the marginal are both the price and all three are one horizontal line.

quiz.question: Nadira Textiles sells 6 rolls a day at $28 each. Its total revenue is:
quiz.explanation: TR = P × Q = $28 × 6 = $168. Notice that this is not the firm's greatest revenue: at 10 rolls it takes $200, despite the lower price.

quiz.question: A firm cuts its price and total revenue rises. Price elasticity of demand at that point must be:
options: between −1.00 and zero
exactly −1.00
below −1.00
positive
quiz.explanation: Revenue rising after a price cut means quantity responded more than price did, which is elastic demand: below −1.00, meaning further from zero. Closer to zero than that a cut lowers revenue, and at −1.00 exactly it leaves revenue unchanged.

quiz.question: Price falls from $30 to $28 and quantity demanded rises from 5 to 6 rolls. Price elasticity of demand is:
quiz.explanation: %ΔQ = +20% and %ΔP = −6.67%, so PED = −3.00. Each percentage is measured against the value it started from; total revenue rises from $150 to $168, as elastic demand requires.

quiz.question: Price elasticity of demand along a straight-line demand curve:
options: is the same everywhere, because the gradient is constant
is elastic at the bottom and inelastic at the top
changes at every point, from elastic at the top to inelastic at the bottom
is undefined except where the curve crosses an axis
quiz.explanation: Elasticity is the gradient combined with the ratio of price to quantity, and that ratio falls all the way down the line. On Nadira Textiles's line the same $2 cut raises revenue at one end and lowers it at the other.

quiz.question: Marginal product crosses average product at:
options: the highest point of average product
the lowest point of average product
the highest point of marginal product
the output where total product stops rising
quiz.explanation: A value above an average pulls it up and a value below pulls it down, so the average can only stop rising at the moment the two are equal. Average product turns downward there, so the crossing is at its highest point.

quiz.question: At Bahri Bottling the wage is $60 a worker a day. When a worker's marginal product is 6 crates, marginal cost is:
quiz.explanation: MC = wage ÷ MP = $60 ÷ 6 = $10. This is the firm's lowest marginal cost, because 6 is its highest marginal product — the two move in opposite directions through the wage.

quiz.question: Under diminishing returns, as more workers are added to a fixed plant:
options: total output keeps rising while the extra output from each worker falls
total output falls with every additional worker
both total output and output per worker rise throughout
the wage the firm has to pay each worker rises
quiz.explanation: It is the marginal product that falls, not total product. Total output usually keeps rising for some way after diminishing returns have set in, which is why "output falls" is the commonest wrong answer here.

quiz.question: Marginal cost passes through average cost at:
options: the lowest point of average fixed cost
the output where average variable cost starts to rise
the lowest point of average cost
the output where marginal cost is at its own lowest
quiz.explanation: While the next unit costs less than the average it pulls the average down, and once it costs more it pulls the average up, so they can only be equal where the average turns. For Bahri Bottling both are $20.

quiz.question: Average fixed cost:
options: is constant at every level of output
falls as output rises and never reaches zero
falls at first and then rises
is zero once fixed costs have been paid
quiz.explanation: AFC = TFC ÷ Q, so a constant is divided by a growing number: it falls forever and approaches zero without arriving. At Bahri Bottling it runs from $30 at 4 crates to $6 at 20.

quiz.question: Bahri Bottling makes 15 crates a day. Its average fixed cost is $8 and its average variable cost is $12. Its average cost is:
quiz.explanation: AC = AFC + AVC at every level of output, because TC = TFC + TVC and all three are divided by the same quantity. $8 + $12 = $20, which is also $300 ÷ 15.

quiz.question: Which of these is a fixed cost for a bottling firm?
options: the bottles and caps used on the line
the wage of a worker hired for one day
the electricity used running the line
the annual insurance on the plant
quiz.explanation: The test is whether the cost changes when output changes, not whether it is large or unavoidable. Insurance arrives whether the line runs or not; the other three arrive only because crates were made.

quiz.question: Minimum efficient scale is:
options: the lowest output at which long-run average cost is at its minimum
the output at which a firm makes the most profit
the smallest output at which a firm can cover its variable costs
the output at which short-run and long-run average cost are equal
quiz.explanation: It is a cost concept and not a profit one. For Bahri Bottling long-run average cost reaches $13 at 50 crates a day and stays there to 70; minimum efficient scale is the FIRST of those outputs.

quiz.question: In the long run:
options: the plant is fixed and only labour can be varied
at least five years have passed since the firm was founded
a firm can no longer change the scale at which it produces
every factor of production can be varied, so there are no fixed costs
quiz.explanation: The two periods are defined by what can change, not by a length of time. How long the long run takes differs completely between an industry renting small units and one that has to build a refinery.

quiz.question: The long-run average cost curve can never lie above a short-run average cost curve because:
options: long-run costs are always lower than short-run costs at every output
fixed costs are excluded from the long-run calculation
the long run assumes the firm has reached minimum efficient scale
in the long run keeping the existing plant is always one of the options
quiz.explanation: The long run contains the short run as a special case: a firm that can change everything can also choose to change nothing. So it can never be forced into a higher cost than a short run would have given it.

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of a TECHNICAL economy of scale?
options: a larger firm borrows at a lower rate of interest than a small one
a supplier quotes a lower price a unit for a larger order
a full-time specialist manager becomes worth employing
a machine that only pays for itself at high output spreads its cost over more units
quiz.explanation: The six internal sources are financial, technical, managerial, marketing, purchasing and risk bearing. The other three options here are the financial, purchasing and managerial economies, each with its own mechanism.

quiz.question: External economies of scale differ from internal ones because they:
options: are always larger than internal economies of scale
only ever affect firms that are already very large
arise from a firm buying its inputs from outside suppliers
arise from the growth of the industry rather than of the firm itself
quiz.explanation: The test is whose growth caused the saving. A firm that has not grown at all can gain an external economy when the industry around it grows, and it loses one by moving away however large it is — which is what makes them less reliable than internal economies.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the three sources of diseconomies of scale the specification names?
options: a rise in the wage the firm has to pay
the law of diminishing returns
a fall in demand for the product
X-inefficiency
quiz.explanation: The three are communication problems, coordination problems and X-inefficiency, and all three are about the firm becoming harder to run. Diminishing returns are a short-run effect from a fixed factor and are not a diseconomy of scale.

quiz.question: A firm in the long run finds its average cost per unit rising as it grows. This is:
options: the law of diminishing returns
diseconomies of scale
an external economy of scale
average fixed cost rising
quiz.explanation: In the long run nothing is fixed, so diminishing returns cannot be the cause — they need a fixed factor for the variable factor to be spread over. And average fixed cost cannot rise, because in the long run there is none.

quiz.question: In the short run a firm should shut down if:
options: price is below average variable cost
price is below average cost
it is making a loss of any size
price is below average fixed cost
quiz.explanation: The fixed cost is owed whether the firm produces or not, so the comparison is between two losses. While price covers average variable cost, each unit leaves something towards the fixed cost; below it, each unit adds to the loss.

quiz.question: A firm's average cost is $20 and its average variable cost is $12, on fixed costs of $120 a day. Facing a price of $16, in the short run it should:
options: shut down, because it is making a loss of $60
keep producing, because it is making a profit of $60
shut down, because price is below average cost of $20
keep producing, losing $60 rather than $120
quiz.explanation: Revenue is $240 against a cost of $300, so the loss is $60 — smaller than the $120 it would lose by stopping. Price $16 is above average variable cost $12, so each crate contributes towards the fixed cost.

quiz.question: In the long run a firm leaves the industry if price is below:
options: average variable cost
average cost
average fixed cost
marginal cost
quiz.explanation: In the long run every factor can be varied, so there are no fixed costs and nothing to contribute towards. The comparison becomes revenue against total cost, which is the average cost test.

quiz.question: A firm is earning supernormal profit. This means:
options: average revenue is above average variable cost
it is earning more than it did last year
average revenue is above average cost
total revenue is above total fixed cost
quiz.explanation: Supernormal profit is a return over and above normal profit, which is where AR = AC. Covering average variable cost only keeps the firm producing in the short run; it is a long way below supernormal profit.

practice.question: Define the term 'marginal revenue'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate things to say, and the second is not a rewording of the first. Before you write, settle what KIND of quantity this term names, because the two marks hang off that choice and an answer that gets it wrong cannot pick either of them up on the way.
Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue (1 mark) resulting from the sale of one additional unit of output (1 mark). An answer that says "the revenue from the last unit sold" gives the first half and not the second, because it does not make clear that the figure is a change in the TOTAL and not the price the last unit fetched — which are different numbers whenever the price has to fall to sell more.

practice.question: Nadira Textiles faces the demand curve P = 40 − 2Q, where Q is rolls a day. Calculate its total revenue at 6 rolls, its marginal revenue at that output, and the output at which total revenue is greatest. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Three figures are wanted and the third depends on knowing a relationship rather than on substituting into a formula, so do the first two first and let them show you what the third needs. Appendix 6 advises showing workings for a Calculate, and here the workings are what let a marker follow you to the third figure even if the arithmetic slips on the way. Write the demand equation down before you start substituting into it.
Price at 6 rolls is 40 − 2 × 6 = $28 (1 mark), so total revenue is $28 × 6 = $168 (1 mark). Marginal revenue on a straight-line demand curve is MR = 40 − 4Q, so at 6 rolls it is $16 (1 mark). Total revenue is greatest where marginal revenue is $0: 40 − 4Q = 0 gives Q = 10 rolls (1 mark), where total revenue is $200. Setting AR rather than MR to zero is the commonest error and gives 20 rolls, the output at which the firm takes nothing at all.

practice.question: Nadira Textiles cuts its price from $10 to $8 a roll and the quantity it sells rises from 15 to 16 rolls a day. Calculate the price elasticity of demand. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks, and the second is for the number rather than the method, so the method has to be visible for the first one to be safe. Be careful which value each percentage change is measured against: taking either of them against the new figure instead of the starting one gives an answer close enough to look right and far enough to be wrong. Quantitative skill QS8 asks for the calculation and the interpretation, so decide before you finish what the number tells you.
%ΔQ = (16 − 15) ÷ 15 = +6.67% and %ΔP = ($8 − $10) ÷ $10 = −20.00% (1 mark). PED = −0.33 (1 mark). Demand is inelastic here, so the price cut lowers total revenue, from $150 to $128. Dropping the minus sign loses nothing on its own but makes the interpretation impossible to state.

practice.question: Explain why a firm facing inelastic demand for its product would not raise its total revenue by cutting its price. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Explain of a reason needs a two-stage chain, so plan both links before writing. The first link is about what inelastic demand means for the size of the quantity response; the second is about what that does to the two numbers total revenue is made of. Keep the percentage changes as percentages throughout — this answer collapses the moment it starts comparing a number of units with a number of dollars.
Inelastic demand means price elasticity of demand lies between zero and minus one, so the percentage rise in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage fall in price (1 mark). Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity, so a cut changes both (1 mark). The gain from selling more units is smaller than the loss from charging less on every unit (1 mark), so total revenue falls rather than rises (1 mark). An answer that says "demand is inelastic so revenue falls" has asserted the conclusion without the middle two links, which are where the marks are.

practice.question: Analyse how the law of diminishing returns shapes a firm's short-run marginal cost curve. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
An Analyse wants depth rather than breadth, so take one chain all the way rather than describing several things that are true.
